title: The schools, reviewed

segments.voice: Yesterday, the reports, and your line: the chain holds. A chain and a text, tested before trusted. Did you stop to ask where something came from before you passed it on? Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.

A caliph, tradition says, once came to Imam Malik of Medina with an offer. Malik had gathered his book of reports and rulings, the Muwatta. The caliph wanted copies sent to every province, with orders that everyone follow it and nothing else. One book, one law, no more arguments. Malik turned him down. The companions of the Prophet, he said, had spread out to many lands, and the people in each place had already heard reports and acted on them. Let them keep what they have. Today, the schools of law again: why Muslims kept more than one.
screen: `ONE BOOK FOR EVERY PROVINCE?` → `MALIK SAID NO.` → `WHY MORE THAN ONE SCHOOL.`

segments.voice: First, the path and the map. Shari'ah is the path Allah set. Fiqh is the scholars' understanding of it, human work, done with care. A school, a madhhab, is a tradition of that understanding, carried from teacher to student. Second, the same sources. Every school begins with the Qur'an, then the sunnah. Sunni schools add the agreement of scholars and reasoning by likeness. Ja'fari jurists, followed by Twelver Shia, count reason itself as a source alongside the Qur'an, the sunnah and consensus. Third, the names. The year walked through them one by one: Hanafi, from Abu Hanifa in Kufa; Maliki, from Malik in Medina; Shafi'i; Hanbali, from Ahmad ibn Hanbal in Baghdad; Ja'fari, named for Ja'far al-Sadiq; Zaydi, in Yemen; Ibadi, in Oman; and Zahiri, the school of the plain sense. A statement of scholars called the Amman Message named these eight schools and forbade declaring their followers unbelievers. Fourth, why they differ. Scholars received different reports, read words in different ways, weighed methods differently, and all of them were seeking the same thing: what Allah asks. A saying the year met calls that difference a mercy; some attribute it to early scholars rather than to the Prophet. So when one person in a prayer row folds his hands high and the next folds them low, neither is a mistake waiting to be fixed. Each is a school's careful answer, the kind Malik chose to leave in place. The row holds them all, shoulder to shoulder, facing one direction.
screen: `THE PATH, AND THE SCHOLARS' MAP.` · `THE SAME SOURCES, WEIGHED DIFFERENTLY.` · `HANAFI TO ZAHIRI: EIGHT NAMED.` · `DIFFERENT ANSWERS, ONE DIRECTION.`

segments.voice: The practice: pray beside someone of another school. Start in the sit. Settle, and breathe. Bring back Malik's answer: let them keep what they have. Let it settle. If you pray at a mosque this week, you can stand next to someone whose prayer looks different from yours, and simply pray, without a word about it afterward. If you don't pray, think of one person whose practice differs from yours in a small way, and let it be their careful answer, not a mistake. The bell holds the time.
The schools. Traditions of fiqh, human understanding of the divine law, each built from the same sources and each still standing in the same row. Today's word.

Your line: many schools, one row. Today, when you notice someone doing a familiar thing differently, ask yourself what careful reason they might have, before you decide anything. Tomorrow, the creed, reviewed. Day one thousand four hundred fourteen.

howItsDone: A Muslim may follow one school of law, learned from family, a mosque or a teacher, and Muslims of different schools pray side by side in the same congregation, each following their own school's details.
